strategies.name: Transit Oriented Development
strategies.short_description: Higher-density mixed-use development around high-quality transit. Residents shift commute trips to transit at a rate documented by CAPCOA T-3.
strategies.extended_description:
Transit-oriented development places compact, mixed-use development within walking
distance of high-quality transit, typically around a rail station or major bus hub.
Locating residents near frequent transit can increase transit commuting and reduce
driving compared with accommodating the same residents in a less transit-accessible
development pattern. Nearby jobs, shops, and services can provide additional benefits by
allowing some daily trips to be made without driving.

Adding homes, jobs, and activity around a station can still increase total trips and total
VMT within the project area. This strategy should therefore not be interpreted as showing
that a new development will reduce overall VMT compared with today. The calculator
estimates reduced driving among those traveling to and from the TOD walkshed compared with
the baseline. Benefits are greatest where frequent transit, safe walking routes, connected
streets, and parking management make driving less necessary.
strategies.guidance:
Use this strategy to compare development around an existing or planned
high-quality transit station with otherwise similar development in a non-TOD area. For
density that is not associated with a transit station, use
[Increased Residential
Density](#/strategies/residential_density)
or [Increased Employment
Density](#/strategies/employment_density)
instead.
strategies.impact_qualifier: relative to the baseline travel pattern
strategies.method: CAPCOA T-3 (Transit-Oriented Development); Lund 2004 / Cervero 2007 / Chatman 2013
strategies.methodology_detail:
Living within walking distance of high-quality transit leads residents to ride
transit far more and drive far less, lowering vehicle miles traveled (VMT). The
calculator gives residents inside the walkshed a transit share equal to the
area's transit share times a multiplier (4.9× by default, the typical rail-station
value), capped at 50% as a realistic ceiling. This follows CAPCOA
[T-3 (Provide Transit-Oriented Development)](https://www.caleemod.com/documents/handbook/ch_3_transportation/measure_t-3.pdf),
drawing on Lund (2004), Cervero (2007), and Chatman (2013).

`ΔVMT% = −%TAZ_in_TOD × (min(TOD_ratio × transit_MS, cap) − transit_MS) / auto_MS`

The effect grows with the share of the area's population that lives inside the
walkshed. Commute mode share comes from American Community Survey (ACS) data.
Lower the multiplier for development served by bus only, which shifts fewer trips
than rail.

applicability.warn_message: Transit-oriented development depends on high-quality transit, which is generally limited to urban and suburban areas.

inputs.label: Share of TAZ within TOD walkshed
inputs.summary: The share of the project area's population that is expected to live inside the ½-mile walkshed around the station, based on planned TOD housing.
inputs.source_note: your development program / site plan vs. the TAZ population
inputs.tooltip: Share of the area's population estimated to live within the ½-mi transit-oriented development walkshed.
inputs.instructions:
Estimate the share of the TAZ's population that will live inside the TOD
walkshed, roughly the ½-mile area around the station that is comfortable to
walk. Compare the planned TOD housing (or population) against the TAZ total.
If the TOD covers only part of a large TAZ, this share is small.

inputs.label: TOD transit-MS multiplier
inputs.summary: The transit mode-share multiplier for the TOD; keep 4.9x for a rail station, or lower it (2-3x) for a bus-served TOD.
inputs.source_note: the transit service serving your TOD (rail vs. bus)
inputs.tooltip: CAPCOA T-3 default = 4.9× (rail-station TODs). Lower for bus-served TODs.
inputs.instructions:
Leave at the 4.9× default for development around a rail station (the CAPCOA
T-3 value). Lower it for TODs served by bus only, which shift fewer trips; a
2–3× multiplier is more realistic for frequent bus service.

strategies.name: Transit Pass Subsidies
strategies.short_description: Reduce the price of transit passes for residents or targeted users, raising ridership and shifting trips off the road.
strategies.extended_description:
This measure reduces the out-of-pocket cost of riding by offering discounted or
free passes to residents, students, lower-income riders, or other eligible community
members. When transit is less expensive and easily accessible, some trips may shift from
driving to transit.

The effect depends on who receives the subsidy and whether transit serves the trips
those users need to make. Implementing this measure in areas with high-quality transit is
likely to have a stronger effect than implementing the same measure in places where
service is infrequent or indirect.
strategies.guidance:
Use this strategy when a transit agency, public program, or other sponsor
reduces fares for the broader riding public. For transit passes provided to employees or
occupants of a development, such as an RTD EcoPass, use [Employer-Provided Commute
Benefits](#/strategies/employee_commuting_benefits),
which applies the effect specifically to commute trips.
strategies.method: Paulley (2006) short-run fare elasticity (ε=−0.30), all trips
strategies.methodology_detail:
Lowering the fare draws more riders onto transit, and some of those trips would
otherwise have been made by car, so vehicle miles traveled (VMT) fall. A larger
fare reduction reaching more riders produces a bigger shift. This follows CAPCOA
[T-29 (Reduce Transit Fares)](https://www.caleemod.com/documents/handbook/ch_3_transportation/measure_t-29.pdf)
and the fare-response relationship in Paulley et al. (2006).

`ΔVMT% = (Δfare × eligible × ε × transit_MS × 1/AVO) / auto_MS`

The calculator uses local commute mode share from the American Community Survey
(ACS), with statewide averages for vehicle occupancy and the typical fare. If you
know the subsidy in dollars rather than a percentage, divide it by the average
fare to get the percentage reduction.

applicability.warn_message: Fare reductions work where transit is a viable option; in rural areas with little service the effect is minimal.

inputs.label: Fare reduction
inputs.summary: The percent reduction in the effective fare riders pay (50% for half-price passes, 100% for free); a dollar subsidy divided by the average fare gives this percentage.
inputs.source_note: your transit agency's fare and pass-subsidy data
inputs.tooltip: Percent reduction in the effective fare (50% = half-price passes; 100% = free).
inputs.instructions:
Enter the percentage reduction in the effective fare riders pay. A half-price
pass program is 50%; a fully subsidized (free) pass is 100%. If you know the
subsidy in dollars instead, divide it by the average fare to get the percentage.

inputs.label: Share of riders eligible
inputs.summary: The share of area transit riders eligible for the subsidized passes, a subset for a targeted program (students, low-income) and approaching 100% for a universal one.
inputs.source_note: your project scope / eligible-population estimate
inputs.tooltip: Share of area transit users covered by the subsidy.
inputs.instructions:
Estimate the percentage of transit riders in the project area who would be eligible
for the reduced fare. A program limited to students, income-qualified riders, or
another specific group will cover only part of the transit-riding population, while
a program available to all riders may approach 100%.

inputs.label: VMT scope
inputs.tooltip: Apply the reduction to all VMT, or only to commute VMT.
inputs.summary: Whether the subsidy's reduction applies to all VMT or only commute VMT.
inputs.instructions:
Choose whether this fare subsidy reduces all vehicle travel or only commute
travel. Pick "Commute trips only" for an employer- or commute-focused pass
program; pick "All trips" for a general, population-wide fare reduction.

strategies.name: Transit Service Frequency Increase
strategies.short_description: More frequent service (shorter waits) on existing transit routes, drawing riders out of cars.
strategies.extended_description:
Transit service frequency improvements reduce the scheduled headway (the time between
arriving buses or trains) on an existing transit corridor. Shorter waits make transit
easier to use, reduce scheduling challenges, and can make transit more time effective.

The benefit depends on the existing service level, the size of the improvement, corridor
demand, and reliability. More frequent service on a high-demand route will generally
produce a larger response than small improvements spread across routes with limited
demand.
strategies.guidance:
Use this strategy for existing service frequency increases. For implementation of new
routes, route extensions, or new service, use the
[Transit Service Expansion](#/strategies/new_transit_service)
strategy instead.
strategies.method: Handy 2013 frequency elasticity (ε=0.5)
strategies.methodology_detail:
When transit comes more often, riders spend less time waiting and more people
choose transit over driving, lowering vehicle miles traveled (VMT). The bigger the
improvement in frequency, the larger the ridership gain. This follows CAPCOA
[T-26 (Increase Transit Service Frequency)](https://www.caleemod.com/documents/handbook/ch_3_transportation/measure_t-26.pdf)
and the frequency relationship in Handy et al. (2013).

`ΔVMT% = −L × Δfreq × transit_MS × ε × (1/AVO) / auto_MS`

The calculator uses local commute mode share from the American Community Survey
(ACS) and a statewide average for vehicle occupancy. Use the implementation level
to phase in a change that isn't fully in place yet.

applicability.warn_message: Frequency improvements deliver the most benefit where transit ridership is already established; in rural areas the effect is minimal.

inputs.label: Frequency change
inputs.summary: The percent change in how often service will operate compared with the existing service. This percentage will be positive for more frequent service, and it will be negative for a service cut.
inputs.tooltip: Positive percentage = more frequent service; negative percentage = service frequency reduction.
inputs.instructions:
Enter the percentage change in how often service runs on the affected routes. If
service improves from every 30 minutes to every 20 minutes, frequency increases
by 50% (30 ÷ 20 − 1); if it improves from every 60 minutes to every 30 minutes,
frequency increases by 100% (60 ÷ 30 − 1). Compare the planned trips per hour (or
vehicles per day) against the current schedule on the routes that overlap with the
selected project area. Use a negative value to model a service cut.

To check the existing transit routes, operators, and service in your area,
access CDOT's
[Statewide Transit Routes map](https://cdot.maps.arcgis.com/home/item.html?id=dd812c7abb8e4017bc83e2cf9ef54824)
or your local transit agency's service plan.

strategies.name: Transit Shelters
strategies.short_description: Shelters and station amenities that make waiting for transit more comfortable, raising ridership.
strategies.extended_description:
Transit shelters and station improvements (covered seating, lighting, real-time arrival
information, and other amenities) make waiting for transit more comfortable. Transit
shelters provide covered waiting areas that make using transit more comfortable and
convenient, particularly during poor weather. Improved waiting conditions can support a
modest increase in transit ridership, including some trips that would otherwise have been
made by driving, reducing vehicle miles traveled.

The effect depends on how many stops are improved and on the area's existing transit mode
share, and shelters add the most where transit is already a viable option. Shelters are a
station-improvement amenity within the broader transit toolkit, and they are best paired
with the calculator's transit service frequency and fare reduction strategies.
strategies.guidance:
Use this strategy for projects that add or upgrade transit shelters and stop
amenities. Do not combine this strategy with the Bus Rapid Transit coverage configuration
below. This configuration option includes BRT station amenities as part of the BRT corridor
investment.
strategies.method: CAPCOA T-46 (structural; constants pending fact-sheet confirmation)
strategies.methodology_detail:
Transit shelters and station improvements raise transit's attractiveness, producing a
small ridership gain that converts to a vehicle miles traveled (VMT) reduction through the
same ridership-to-VMT machinery as CAPCOA
[T-26 (Increase Transit Service Frequency)](https://www.caleemod.com/documents/handbook/ch_3_transportation/measure_t-26.pdf),
following Measure
[T-46 (Provide Transit Shelters)](https://www.caleemod.com/documents/handbook/ch_3_transportation/measure_t-46.pdf):

`ΔVMT% = −(LOI × ridership_uplift × transit_MS × (1/AVO) / vehicle_MS)`, capped at the 15%
Transit subsector maximum.

The mode-shift factor uses the area's **observed** average vehicle occupancy (1/AVO) rather
than the national default, and local transit and vehicle mode shares come from the area
data. T-46 is **mutually exclusive with Bus Rapid Transit** where BRT covers all community
routes, and turning on that flag zeroes the credit.

> **Constants pending confirmation.** The verbatim T-46 equation and constants (the
> shelter ridership uplift and the measure maximum) were not captured during research and
> the fact sheet was unreadable at implementation time. The ridership uplift and measure
> maximum are **placeholders** exposed in the code (`TRANSIT_SHELTERS_T46`) for
> recalibration and should be confirmed against the T-46 fact sheet before the numeric
> results are relied upon. Outputs flag this assumption.

**Sources**

- CAPCOA *Handbook* (2021), Measure
  [T-46 (Provide Transit Shelters)](https://www.caleemod.com/documents/handbook/ch_3_transportation/measure_t-46.pdf);
  conversion machinery from Measure
  [T-26](https://www.caleemod.com/documents/handbook/ch_3_transportation/measure_t-26.pdf).
- Handy, S., et al. (2013). *Impacts of Transit Service Strategies on Passenger Vehicle Use
  and GHG Emissions*. CARB.

strategies.name: Unbundled Parking for Multifamily Housing
strategies.short_description: Renting or selling parking spaces separately from housing units.
strategies.extended_description:
Unbundled parking for multifamily housing separates the cost of parking from the cost of
renting or purchasing a housing unit. Instead of including parking as part of the housing
cost, residents rent or buy parking spaces separately. This saves money for residents who
do not have a car, and it reduces the incentive for households to own or store multiple
vehicles on site.

The effect of unbundled parking will vary based on neighborhood context, parking supply,
parking pricing, and access to transportation options. It is most effective in areas with
strong transit, walking, biking, carshare, or micromobility options, where residents can
realistically choose to live car-free or car-light. In areas with limited transportation
alternatives or abundant free off-site parking, the VMT reduction potential may be lower
unless unbundled parking is paired with other TDM measures.
strategies.guidance:
Use this strategy for multifamily residential projects or policies that price
parking separately from housing costs. It is most appropriate where residents have
realistic alternatives to owning or using a vehicle, such as transit, walking, biking,
carshare, or micromobility. For employee parking pricing or cash-out programs, use
[Workplace Parking
Pricing](#/strategies/workplace_parking_pricing)
or [Parking
Cash-Out](#/strategies/parking_cashout)
instead.
strategies.method: CAPCOA T-16 (parking price-elasticity; 15.7% cap)
strategies.methodology_detail:
Unbundling separates the price of a parking space from the dwelling price, so residents pay
for parking only if they keep a vehicle. Revealing the cost lowers car ownership and shifts
trips to other modes, reducing household vehicle miles traveled (VMT). Following CAPCOA
[T-16 (Unbundle Residential Parking Costs from Property Cost)](https://www.caleemod.com/documents/handbook/ch_3_transportation/measure_t-16.pdf),
the unbundled charge is a price signal relative to the residents' cost of vehicle
ownership, scaled by the parking-demand price elasticity of **−0.4** (Lehner & Peirson
2019):

`ΔVMT% = −(unbundled_parking_charge / reference_cost) × −0.4 × adjustment_factors`

capped at the **15.7% measure maximum** (confirmed: Caltrans SB 743 Playbook; USDOT 2025).

**Mandatory condition:** the measure "will not work if free parking is readily available on
the street or elsewhere near the housing project." When that is the case, the strategy
returns **zero**, because unbundling only changes behavior if residents can't simply park free
nearby.

> **Constants pending confirmation.** The CAPCOA T-16 fact sheet could not be read at
> implementation time. The reference-cost denominator (defaulted to the annual vehicle
> ownership cost basis) and the adjustment factor are **placeholders** exposed in the code
> (`UNBUNDLE_RESIDENTIAL_T16`); confirm against the fact sheet, including whether CAPCOA
> uses a fee→reduction lookup table or the closed-form elasticity used here. The 15.7% cap
> is confirmed. Outputs flag this.

**Sources**

- CAPCOA *Handbook*, Measure
  [T-16 (Unbundle Residential Parking Costs)](https://www.caleemod.com/documents/handbook/ch_3_transportation/measure_t-16.pdf),
  pp. 126–129.
- Caltrans *SB 743 Program Mitigation Playbook* (15.7% cap; free-parking caveat).
- Lehner & Peirson (2019), parking price elasticity (−0.4).
- USDOT (2025), *Parking Reforms* (~15% figure).

applicability.warn_message: Effective only where free parking is not readily available nearby and residents have viable non-car options; results use placeholder constants pending CAPCOA T-16 confirmation.

strategies.name: Commuter Vanpool
strategies.short_description: Employer-supported or regional vanpools that consolidate commute trips into a single high-occupancy vehicle.
strategies.extended_description:
Vanpools bring together commuters with similar origins, destinations, and schedules to
share a vehicle, replacing several drive-alone commute trips with one vanpool trip. They
are generally most effective for longer commutes, shift-based workplaces, and locations
that are not well served by fixed-route transit.

The effect depends on whether enough commuters have compatible schedules and travel
patterns. A vanpool serving a long commute to a major employment site can reduce more
vehicle miles than one serving short trips or dispersed schedules, and successful
programs require rider matching and reliable vehicle operations.
strategies.guidance:
Use this strategy for implementation of employer-, agency-, or regionally
supported commuter vanpool programs. Enter the share of area commute trips the program can
realistically reach and how fully the program is implemented.
strategies.method: Effect-size adaptation of TCRP 95 service-miles elasticity, commute scope (cf. CAPCOA T-11)
strategies.methodology_detail:
Each vanpool takes several commuters out of their own cars and into one shared
vehicle, reducing commute vehicle miles traveled (VMT). The reduction grows with
the share of the area's commute trips the program carries and how fully it is
running. The approach mirrors CAPCOA
[T-11 (Provide Employer-Sponsored Vanpool)](https://www.caleemod.com/documents/handbook/ch_3_transportation/measure_t-11.pdf).

`Δcommute_VMT% = −%trips_impacted × Δservice × transit_MS × ε × 1/AVO`

The calculator uses a statewide average of 1.20 people per vehicle (2017 National
Household Travel Survey, NHTS). Regional vanpool participation is usually small, so
base the share reached on observed local numbers rather than a target.

inputs.summary: The share of the area's commute trips the vanpool program will carry. This is typically just a percent or two of all area commute trips; use existing vanpool participation rates rather than an aspirational target.

Regional participation is typically small (a percent or two), so use existing
vanpool participation rates if available (for example, DRCOG's Way to Go Vanpool
Program publishes participation information for the DRCOG region) rather than an
aspirational target.

strategies.name: Wayfinding
strategies.short_description: Signage and navigation tools that help people easily find routes, destinations, and transportation options.
strategies.extended_description:
Wayfinding improvements help people navigate to key destinations using clear routes and
directions. Wayfinding can include directional signage, maps, pavement markings, artwork,
and other visual identifiers. For the purposes of this tool, wayfinding estimates the
potential VMT reductions associated with making walking, biking, and transit connections
easier to understand and navigate.

The effect of wayfinding will vary based on the strength of the underlying transportation
network and the ease of using the system. Wayfinding is most effective when paired with
improvements to the active transportation network, transit access, or first/last-mile
connections, especially for users who may be unfamiliar with traveling through the
community in this way.
strategies.guidance:
Use this strategy where a project helps people understand how to navigate
between key destinations while walking, biking, or rolling. Wayfinding should primarily be
modeled when it supports an existing or planned multimodal network; it will not have a
major impact on its own without multimodal improvements.
strategies.method: Derived, two-channel (assumption-bounded)
strategies.methodology_detail:
**No empirical VMT effect size exists for wayfinding in any mode.** Every credible source
treats wayfinding as a quality/legibility sub-feature of a larger transit or active-mode
investment, never a standalone strategy. This method credits it only as a small, capped,
mode-specific friction-reduction uplift, routed through established CAPCOA conversion
machinery, with a deliberately conservative assumed uplift.

Two channels combine multiplicatively:

- **Transit legibility**, routed through the CAPCOA
  [T-26](https://www.caleemod.com/documents/handbook/ch_3_transportation/measure_t-26.pdf)
  ridership-to-VMT conversion:
  `ch_transit = LOI_transit × 0.25% × transit_MS × (1/AVO) / vehicle_MS`, where the
  mode-shift factor uses the area's observed average vehicle occupancy (AVO).
- **Active-mode legibility**, routed through the CAPCOA
  [T-18](https://www.caleemod.com/documents/handbook/ch_3_transportation/measure_t-18.pdf)
  pedestrian elasticity as a usability multiplier on the *existing* bike/ped network:
  `ch_active = LOI_active × 0.25% × |−0.05|`.

Each channel is capped at 0.5%. The assumed 0.25%-per-channel uplift is a conservative,
client-selected default exposed for recalibration. Critically, each channel is
**parent-gated**: the transit channel is credited only where transit service exists and
the active channel only where a bike/ped network exists. If the parent investment is
absent, that channel returns 0.

This estimate is **assumption-based, not empirically derived**, and wayfinding should not
be claimed as an independent strategy. The active-mode channel is the weaker analogy: the
−0.05 elasticity is borrowed structure, not a measured wayfinding effect.

**Sources (borrowed conversion machinery only, not wayfinding effect sizes)**

- CAPCOA *Handbook* (2021), Measure
  [T-26 (Increase Transit Service Frequency)](https://www.caleemod.com/documents/handbook/ch_3_transportation/measure_t-26.pdf)
  and Measure
  [T-18 (Provide Pedestrian Network Improvement)](https://www.caleemod.com/documents/handbook/ch_3_transportation/measure_t-18.pdf).

applicability.warn_message: Wayfinding has no standalone empirical effect; it is credited only as a small, capped uplift where a transit or bike/ped network already exists.

strategies.name: Workplace Parking Pricing
strategies.short_description: Charge employees for parking at work (or remove free parking) to discourage driving alone for the commute.
strategies.extended_description:
Workplace parking pricing charges employees for parking at work or removes an existing
free-parking benefit. Making employees responsible for some or all of the parking cost can
encourage them to consider lower-cost commute options such as transit, carpooling,
vanpooling, bicycling, walking, or telework.

This strategy may also include parking cash-out, in which employees who give up an
employer-provided parking space receive a payment or other commute benefit instead.

The effect depends on the parking price, the availability of free or lower-cost parking
nearby, and whether employees have practical alternatives to driving alone. Pricing is
generally most effective at worksites with limited parking, strong travel options, and
clear information about available commute choices.
strategies.guidance:
This strategy applies to commute trips and should generally be used for
employees who currently receive free, subsidized, or underpriced workplace parking. For
priced public or curb parking across an area, use [Parking Fees and Curb
Management](#/strategies/parking_fees_curb_management).
strategies.method: Lehner & Peer (2019) parking demand elasticity (ε=−0.40), commute scope
strategies.methodology_detail:
Charging for parking that used to be free raises the cost of driving to work, so
some employees carpool, switch modes, or stop driving alone, reducing commute
vehicle miles traveled (VMT). The larger the price increase and the more employees
it reaches, the bigger the reduction, following CAPCOA
[T-12 (Price Workplace Parking)](https://www.caleemod.com/documents/handbook/ch_3_transportation/measure_t-12.pdf)
and the parking-response relationship in Lehner & Peer (2019).

`Δcommute_VMT% = %Δprice × ε × share_affected`

Where parking is free today, introducing a charge is treated as a meaningful price
increase. By default the strategy covers the share of employees who already pay to
park in this type of area; set it directly if you know how many worksites the
pricing reaches. The estimate is most reliable for moderate price changes and
overstates the response to very large ones (above about a 50% increase).

applicability.warn_message: Parking pricing changes behavior where parking is constrained and alternatives exist; it has little effect in rural areas with abundant free parking.
